In Thymesia, players control Corvus, a faceless hero clad in a Medieval plague doctor outfit. The story is set in the realm of Hermes, which tried to use alchemy to contain a rapidly expanding plague, an approach that proved to be more harm than good, as it ended up mutating Hermes' denizens into horrific monsters. The Map Is Drawn
Your World Is…

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life
looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in
return.
The Rings of Power · Prime Video · Since 2022
Middle-earth

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and
somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right
thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

This is the only world on the list where doing good is understood as a very long defeat,
fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

The Rings of Power is set in the last good age before it all goes wrong, which gives
every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.
You would take the hard road, and you would take it on foot.
One Piece · Manga since 1997 · Netflix 2023
The Grand Line

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where
you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

One Piece has run for decades on one very simple engine, which is a group of people who
each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

The world is enormous and deliberately ridiculous, and the emotional gut punches land
harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

You would set sail knowing the map runs out, which is more or less the entire point of
it.
The Witcher · Netflix · Since 2019
The Continent

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The
Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

Witchers get paid to do what nobody else will and resented for existing at all, which is
a trade most people would refuse and you would probably accept.

You have no real illusions about which side is the good one, largely because on the
Continent that question tends to have a disappointing answer.

The best of these stories are not about the fighting. They are about somebody with a
rigid code being repeatedly cornered into caring about people.

You would take the coin, finish the job properly, and be out of town before the story
got told wrong.
Percy Jackson · Disney+ · Since 2023
Camp Half-Blood

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and
you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as
everybody kept telling you.

Percy Jackson takes the oldest stories we have and drops them into car parks and diners,
which makes the gods considerably funnier and a great deal worse.

You would be the kid every school gave up on, who turns out to have been built for
something nobody thought to test for.

The series is genuinely about friendship rather than destiny, and it says so out loud
every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.

'Mortal Shell' (2020)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/mortal-shell-social.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: A knight in the game Mortal Shell

blocks.x: Image via Playstack

Mortal Shell is a game that's been making headlines recently, mostly due to its brand new sequel, which came out last August. The sequel was a distinct improvement over its predecessor, but the original still has its own charm. When it comes to Soulslike RPGs, you typically create a character, choose a class, and build and tailor your hero to fit a specific playstyle. Mortal Shell does not let you do that.

You start as a faceless, featureless husk of a human being, and must progress through the world by jumping into hollow shells; remnants of warriors long dead. These shells come with weapons, armor, and faces, giving you a proper character. Be warned, though: they are not permanent. They come in various classes, meaning one shell will have you playing as a tank, while another will be based on agility and speed. It's a game that forces you to adapt and think on your feet in its bleak and unforgiving world, which is why it's so brilliant.

3
'Lords of the Fallen' (2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/09/lords-of-the-fallen-dark-crusader-radiance-build-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A character raising a shield in lords-of-the-fallen

blocks.x: Image via CI Games

Lords of the Fallen is a stand-alone sequel to the 2014 Soulslike of the same name. The original was pretty average, but this sequel is an improvement in every possible way. The story is about humanity's struggle against the infernal god Adyr, the Bereft Exile. Adyr's defeat is orchestrated by a rising order called the Hallowed Sentinels, though they are powerless to prevent his imminent resurrection. As a desperate last-ditch effort, a crusader lobs his magic lantern into a pit of bodies, bringing one back from the dead, which is where the player comes in.

The levels are much more open and really intelligently designed, with the various areas interconnecting and overlapping in original Dark Souls fashion. The game also added a mechanic in the form of the aforementioned magical lamp that allows players to switch between the overworld, Axiom, and the parallel dimension known as the Umbral, finding hidden secrets, accessing new areas, and progressing further into the game. It's a really fun game with some killer boss fights and infinite replayability due to all the hidden secrets.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/nioh.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: William Adams faces off against Onryoki in 'Nioh'

blocks.x: Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment

Nioh is the first in a trilogy of games created by the same developers behind Wo Long. As such, it is another historical fantasy, set in the real world. Rather than being about ancient Chinese history, this game focuses on Japan in the Edo Period. You play as real-life explorer William Adams, the first Englishman to set foot in Japan, albeit a highly fictionalized version of him.

Nioh sees players travelling across Japan, which is plagued with demons known as oni, who are being released into the world. These oni come straight from Japanese folklore, and even possess some real historical figures. The game is very different to Soulsborne games: the combat is punishing and more about blocking and parrying than dodging, forcing you to change stances and adapt to enemy types. While this game isn't open world, opting for a traditional mission-based format instead, it's a popular pick for Soulslike fans due to its sheer difficulty and differing gameplay.

'Lies of P' (2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/09/lies-of-p-white-lady-npc.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A masked character wielding a sword in Lies of P

blocks.x: Image via Neowiz

Lies of P is based on Carlo Collodi's novel The Adventures of Pinocchio, which was also adapted into a famous Disney animated musical in 1940. The game is set in the city of Krat, which resembles Belle Époque Paris. Automatons called puppets previously served as laborers and servants to humanity before abruptly slaughtering their masters en masse in an apocalyptic event known as the Puppet Frenzy. To make matters worse, a devastating pandemic begins sweeping through the city, turning the infected into horrific abominations.

In the midst of the chaos, a nearly perfect, human-looking puppet named P (short for Pinocchio) is awoken by the Blue Fairy, Sofia, who asks him to rescue his maker, Geppetto, and save Krat. This game brings a ton of cool mechanics to the formula, including custom weapons and prosthetic arms with different abilities. The worldbuilding is incredible, and it's easily one of the most creative adaptations of a book ever made, which is why it earns the spot as being the best Soulslike RPG in the fantasy genre.

The Map Is Drawn
Your World Is…

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life
looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in
return.

The Rings of Power · Prime Video · Since 2022

Middle-earth

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and
somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right
thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

This is the only world on the list where doing good is understood as a very long defeat,
fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

The Rings of Power is set in the last good age before it all goes wrong, which gives
every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.

You would take the hard road, and you would take it on foot.

One Piece · Manga since 1997 · Netflix 2023

The Grand Line

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where
you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

One Piece has run for decades on one very simple engine, which is a group of people who
each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

The world is enormous and deliberately ridiculous, and the emotional gut punches land
harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

You would set sail knowing the map runs out, which is more or less the entire point of
it.

The Witcher · Netflix · Since 2019

The Continent

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The
Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

Witchers get paid to do what nobody else will and resented for existing at all, which is
a trade most people would refuse and you would probably accept.

You have no real illusions about which side is the good one, largely because on the
Continent that question tends to have a disappointing answer.

The best of these stories are not about the fighting. They are about somebody with a
rigid code being repeatedly cornered into caring about people.

You would take the coin, finish the job properly, and be out of town before the story
got told wrong.

Percy Jackson · Disney+ · Since 2023

Camp Half-Blood

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and
you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as
everybody kept telling you.

Percy Jackson takes the oldest stories we have and drops them into car parks and diners,
which makes the gods considerably funnier and a great deal worse.

You would be the kid every school gave up on, who turns out to have been built for
something nobody thought to test for.

The series is genuinely about friendship rather than destiny, and it says so out loud
every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.

4
'Mortal Shell' (2020)

Image via Playstack

Mortal Shell is a game that's been making headlines recently, mostly due to its brand new sequel, which came out last August. The sequel was a distinct improvement over its predecessor, but the original still has its own charm. When it comes to Soulslike RPGs, you typically create a character, choose a class, and build and tailor your hero to fit a specific playstyle. Mortal Shell does not let you do that.

You start as a faceless, featureless husk of a human being, and must progress through the world by jumping into hollow shells; remnants of warriors long dead. These shells come with weapons, armor, and faces, giving you a proper character. Be warned, though: they are not permanent. They come in various classes, meaning one shell will have you playing as a tank, while another will be based on agility and speed. It's a game that forces you to adapt and think on your feet in its bleak and unforgiving world, which is why it's so brilliant.

3
'Lords of the Fallen' (2023)

Image via CI Games

Lords of the Fallen is a stand-alone sequel to the 2014 Soulslike of the same name. The original was pretty average, but this sequel is an improvement in every possible way. The story is about humanity's struggle against the infernal god Adyr, the Bereft Exile. Adyr's defeat is orchestrated by a rising order called the Hallowed Sentinels, though they are powerless to prevent his imminent resurrection. As a desperate last-ditch effort, a crusader lobs his magic lantern into a pit of bodies, bringing one back from the dead, which is where the player comes in.

The levels are much more open and really intelligently designed, with the various areas interconnecting and overlapping in original Dark Souls fashion. The game also added a mechanic in the form of the aforementioned magical lamp that allows players to switch between the overworld, Axiom, and the parallel dimension known as the Umbral, finding hidden secrets, accessing new areas, and progressing further into the game. It's a really fun game with some killer boss fights and infinite replayability due to all the hidden secrets.

2
'Nioh' (2017)

Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment

Nioh is the first in a trilogy of games created by the same developers behind Wo Long. As such, it is another historical fantasy, set in the real world. Rather than being about ancient Chinese history, this game focuses on Japan in the Edo Period. You play as real-life explorer William Adams, the first Englishman to set foot in Japan, albeit a highly fictionalized version of him.

Nioh sees players travelling across Japan, which is plagued with demons known as oni, who are being released into the world. These oni come straight from Japanese folklore, and even possess some real historical figures. The game is very different to Soulsborne games: the combat is punishing and more about blocking and parrying than dodging, forcing you to change stances and adapt to enemy types. While this game isn't open world, opting for a traditional mission-based format instead, it's a popular pick for Soulslike fans due to its sheer difficulty and differing gameplay.

1
'Lies of P' (2023)

Image via Neowiz

Lies of P is based on Carlo Collodi's novel The Adventures of Pinocchio, which was also adapted into a famous Disney animated musical in 1940. The game is set in the city of Krat, which resembles Belle Époque Paris. Automatons called puppets previously served as laborers and servants to humanity before abruptly slaughtering their masters en masse in an apocalyptic event known as the Puppet Frenzy. To make matters worse, a devastating pandemic begins sweeping through the city, turning the infected into horrific abominations.

In the midst of the chaos, a nearly perfect, human-looking puppet named P (short for Pinocchio) is awoken by the Blue Fairy, Sofia, who asks him to rescue his maker, Geppetto, and save Krat. This game brings a ton of cool mechanics to the formula, including custom weapons and prosthetic arms with different abilities. The worldbuilding is incredible, and it's easily one of the most creative adaptations of a book ever made, which is why it earns the spot as being the best Soulslike RPG in the fantasy genre.
